description: A mixed backlog covering `change-signature` sub-commands plus dogfood-driven workspace-loading, diagnostic-output, interface-segregation, and mutation-safety improvements for `rt`. Stories are ordered so the original change-signature work lands first, followed by infrastructure and analysis improvements uncovered during real repo usage.

userStories.title: change-signature command infrastructure + rename-param sub-command
userStories.description: As a developer, I want `rt change-signature rename-param "Ns.Type.Method" oldName newName` so that I can rename a method parameter and have all named-argument call sites updated automatically.
acceptanceCriteria: A new file `src/RoslynTools/Commands/ChangeSignatureCommand.cs` exists containing an `internal sealed class ChangeSignatureCommand : IRtCommand`.

`ChangeSignatureCommand.Info` is a static `RtCommandInfo` with `Name = "change-signature"`, `Mutates = true`, `JsonOutput = false`, and at least one example invocation referencing the `rename-param` sub-command.
`ChangeSignatureCommand.Build()` returns a `System.CommandLine.Command` named `change-signature` that has `rename-param` registered as a sub-command.
The `rename-param` sub-command accepts positional args `<methodSpec>`, `<oldName>`, `<newName>` and options `--solution` and `--dry-run`.

A new file `src/RoslynTools/Core/ChangeSignatureCore.cs` exists containing an `internal static class ChangeSignatureCore` with `internal static Task<Solution> RenameParamAsync(Solution solution, string methodSpec, string oldName, string newName)`.
Invoking `rename-param` against a method `Foo(int count)` renames the parameter in the declaration to the new name in the resulting Solution.
A named-argument call site `obj.Foo(count: 5)` is rewritten to `obj.Foo(total: 5)` when renaming `count` to `total`.
A positional call site `obj.Foo(5)` is left unchanged when renaming the parameter.
Multiple named-argument call sites across multiple documents in the solution are all updated in a single invocation.
Renaming a constructor parameter updates the constructor declaration and any named-argument `new Type(param: value)` invocations.
Renaming a parameter on a local function updates the local function declaration and any named-argument invocations within its enclosing scope.
Renaming a parameter that does not exist on the target method throws or returns an error indicating the parameter name was not found.
Passing a `methodSpec` that resolves to zero symbols produces an error message identifying the unresolved method spec and exits non-zero.
Passing a `methodSpec` that resolves to multiple overloads triggers the existing disambiguation flow (same contract as `TransformParametersCore`).
Attempting to rename a parameter to a name that conflicts with another parameter on the same method produces a validation error and makes no changes.
Running with `--dry-run` prints a unified diff to stdout, writes no files to disk, and exits 0.
Running without `--dry-run` applies changes via `SolutionWriter.ApplyChangesAsync` and the modified files exist on disk with the new parameter name.
A new test file `tests/RoslynTools.Tests/Mutation/ChangeSignatureTests.cs` exists and uses `AdhocProjectBuilder` for fixtures (no mocking of Roslyn types).
Tests call `ChangeSignatureCore.RenameParamAsync` directly and assert on the returned `Solution` contents.

userStories.title: change-signature reorder sub-command
userStories.description: As a developer, I want `rt change-signature reorder "Ns.Type.Method" "2,0,1"` so that I can reorder method parameters and have all call sites updated to match.
acceptanceCriteria: `ChangeSignatureCommand.Build()` registers a `reorder` sub-command alongside `rename-param`.
The `reorder` sub-command accepts positional args `<methodSpec>` and `<order>` and options `--solution` and `--dry-run`.
`ChangeSignatureCore.ReorderParamsAsync(Solution, string methodSpec, string[] newOrder) -> Solution` exists as an internal static method.
A numeric order string like `"2,0,1"` is parsed into zero-based indices and used to reorder parameters.
A name-based order string like `"c,a,b"` is resolved to indices against the method's current parameter list before rewriting.
A mixed name/index order string produces a clear validation error (or is documented as unsupported and rejected).
Reordering rewrites the method declaration's parameter list in the new order, preserving each parameter's type, modifiers, attributes, and default value.
Positional call-site arguments are reordered to match the new declaration order across all references in the solution.
Named-argument call sites are reordered in source so argument textual order matches new declaration order, while preserving the `name:` labels and values.
Mixed positional+named call sites (positional prefix followed by named tail) are rewritten correctly so that positional args map to the new positions and named args retain their labels.
Reordering a constructor's parameters updates the constructor declaration and all `new Type(...)` invocations.
Reordering a local function's parameters updates the local function declaration and all in-scope invocations.

Methods whose signature includes a `params` array parameter, or call sites that rely on omitted optional arguments, are rejected in v1 with a clear validation error rather than being partially rewritten.
If the order list length does not equal the parameter count, a validation error is raised and no changes are made.
If the order list contains duplicate indices or names, a validation error is raised and no changes are made.
If the order list contains an out-of-range index (negative or >= param count), a validation error is raised and no changes are made.
If the order list references a name that does not match any parameter, a validation error is raised and no changes are made.
An identity reorder (e.g. `"0,1,2"` on a 3-param method) produces a Solution with no textual changes.
An unresolved `methodSpec` produces an error and exits non-zero.
Overload disambiguation uses the shared `SymbolLocator` flow.
Running with `--dry-run` prints a unified diff showing reordered declaration and call sites, writes no files, and exits 0.
Running without `--dry-run` applies changes to disk via `SolutionWriter.ApplyChangesAsync`.

Tests in `ChangeSignatureTests.cs` cover: numeric-index reorder, name-based reorder, positional-only call site, named-only call site, mixed positional+named call site, multiple call sites in the same document, cross-file call sites, constructor reorder, local-function reorder, identity reorder no-op, length-mismatch validation, duplicate-index validation, out-of-range validation, unknown-name validation, and v1 rejection of unsupported `params`/omitted-optional cases.

userStories.title: change-signature add-param and remove-param sub-commands
userStories.description: As a developer, I want `rt change-signature add-param` and `rt change-signature remove-param` so that I can add or remove parameters with call sites updated appropriately.
acceptanceCriteria: `ChangeSignatureCommand.Build()` registers `add-param` and `remove-param` sub-commands.
`add-param` accepts positional args `<methodSpec>` and `<paramSpec>`, plus options `--after <paramName>`, `--solution`, and `--dry-run`.
`remove-param` accepts positional args `<methodSpec>` and `<paramName>`, plus options `--force`, `--solution`, and `--dry-run`.
`ChangeSignatureCore.AddParamAsync(Solution, string methodSpec, string paramSpec, string? afterParam) -> Solution` exists as an internal static method.
`ChangeSignatureCore.RemoveParamAsync(Solution, string methodSpec, string paramName, bool force) -> Solution` exists as an internal static method.
`add-param` parses the `paramSpec` string as a C# parameter declaration (type + identifier + default-value clause) using Roslyn's `SyntaxFactory.ParseParameterList` or equivalent.
A `paramSpec` with no default value (e.g. `"int count"`) is rejected with a validation error explaining that a default value is required.
A `paramSpec` whose parameter name conflicts with an existing parameter on the target method is rejected with a validation error.
`add-param` with no `--after` inserts the new parameter at the end of the declaration's parameter list.
`add-param --after existingParam` inserts the new parameter immediately after the named existing parameter.
`add-param --after nonExistentParam` produces a validation error and makes no changes.
`add-param` does not modify any call sites (existing invocations remain valid because the new parameter has a default).
`add-param` works for methods, constructors, and local functions.
`remove-param` validates that the target parameter has a default value unless `--force` is passed; otherwise it errors and makes no changes.
`remove-param --force` bypasses the declaration-level default-value validation and removes the parameter regardless.
`remove-param` removes the parameter from the declaration, preserving trivia and remaining parameters' formatting.
`remove-param` removes the positional argument at the corresponding index from all call sites across the solution.
`remove-param` removes named arguments matching the removed parameter's name from all call sites.
`remove-param` handles call sites where the argument is positional at some sites and named at others â€” both are removed correctly.
Multiple call sites in the same document are all rewritten correctly in a single invocation without later rewrites using stale spans from earlier edits.
Using `--force` does not suppress rewrite-safety checks: if any invocation shape cannot be safely rewritten, the command exits non-zero and makes no partial changes.
`remove-param` for a parameter that does not exist on the target method produces a validation error.
`remove-param` works for methods, constructors, and local functions.
Unresolved `methodSpec` on either sub-command produces an error and exits non-zero.
Overload disambiguation uses the shared `SymbolLocator` flow for both sub-commands.
Running either sub-command with `--dry-run` prints a unified diff, writes no files, and exits 0.
Running either sub-command without `--dry-run` applies changes to disk via `SolutionWriter.ApplyChangesAsync`.

Tests cover add-param: append at end, insert after named param, after-param-not-found error, missing-default-value error, name-conflict error, method/constructor/local-function targets, and verification that call sites are untouched.

Tests cover remove-param: default-value required validation, `--force` bypass, positional-arg removal at single call site, multiple call sites in the same document, positional-arg removal across multiple files, named-arg removal, mixed positional+named call sites, non-existent param error, rewrite-safety failure under `--force`, and method/constructor/local-function targets.

userStories.title: nearest-solution auto-detection and repo default resolution
userStories.description: As a developer, I want `rt` to resolve the correct solution automatically from my working directory so that I do not have to repeatedly pass `--solution` for routine repo use.
acceptanceCriteria: `WorkspaceLoader.LoadAsync(null)` walks upward from the current working directory when `--solution` is omitted and selects the nearest `.sln` file if exactly one candidate is found on the nearest matching directory level.
If the current directory contains no `.sln` file but a parent directory does, the parent solution is selected and loaded successfully.

If multiple `.sln` files exist on the same nearest directory level, `WorkspaceLoader` fails fast with a clear error that lists the candidate filenames and instructs the user to pass `--solution` explicitly.
If no `.sln` file is found while walking to the filesystem root, `WorkspaceLoader` returns a clear error explaining that no solution was discovered and that `--solution` can be used to override.

A checked-in repo-root file named `.rt-solution` is supported as the repo-level default, containing a relative path to the preferred `.sln` file, and when present it takes precedence over upward auto-detection.
If `.rt-solution` points to a missing file or to a non-`.sln` target, `WorkspaceLoader` returns a validation error naming the invalid configured path and makes no attempt to load a workspace.
An explicit `--solution` argument still takes precedence over repo defaults and auto-detection.
Auto-detection prefers `.sln` files only; passing an explicit `.slnx` path fails fast with a clear unsupported-format error rather than falling through to MSBuildWorkspace.
Commands that already omit `--solution` in tests or examples continue to work with the new resolution behavior without code duplication in individual command classes.

A new test file or updated infrastructure tests cover: nearest-solution resolution from a child directory, parent-directory resolution, multiple-candidate ambiguity, no-solution-found error, `.rt-solution` precedence, invalid `.rt-solution` path error, explicit `--solution` precedence, and explicit `.slnx` rejection.

userStories.notes: Primary touch points: src/RoslynTools/Core/WorkspaceLoader.cs and tests/RoslynTools.Tests/Infrastructure/WorkspaceLoaderSmokeTests.cs. Keep command surface unchanged; centralize behavior in WorkspaceLoader. Use a repo-root `.rt-solution` file containing a relative `.sln` path rather than any user-machine global state.

userStories.title: separate exploration results from non-fatal workspace diagnostics
userStories.description: As a developer, I want `rt` exploration commands to distinguish symbol results from workspace warnings so that I can trust usable semantic output even when restore, audit, or file-lock issues are present.
acceptanceCriteria: Workspace diagnostics captured during `MSBuildWorkspace` loading are classified using an explicit rule: `WorkspaceDiagnosticKind.Warning` is non-fatal, `WorkspaceDiagnosticKind.Failure` is a hard-failure signal unless usable semantic results are already available and the command explicitly degrades to warnings.

When a read-only command such as `inspect`, `find-refs`, `find-callers`, `find-unused`, or `outline` successfully produces semantic results, those results are emitted in the normal output channel without being interleaved line-by-line with workspace diagnostic text.
Non-fatal diagnostics are rendered separately from symbol results, either in a trailing warning section or a structured side channel, so a consumer can distinguish them without parsing mixed output.
Transient restore or package-audit warnings that do not prevent Roslyn from loading semantic information are marked non-fatal and do not cause the command to exit non-zero by themselves.
Hard-failure conditions that prevent solution loading still cause the command to fail fast and exit non-zero with actionable error text.
Informational progress messages such as solution loading banners are not written to stderr during successful read-only exploration runs.
PowerShell invocation with `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` no longer treats successful exploration commands as terminating failures solely because informational text was written to stderr.

At least one integration-style test exercises a workspace load that emits a warning but still returns usable results, and asserts that the primary results remain intact while diagnostics are separated.
At least one test exercises a true workspace load failure and asserts that the command exits non-zero with no misleading partial-success framing.
Existing command output contracts remain backward-compatible for successful result bodies aside from the new diagnostic separation behavior.

userStories.description: As a developer, I want `rt analyze-interface <Interface>` to group consumers by the exact interface members they use so that I can drive interface-segregation work from evidence instead of raw reference dumps.
acceptanceCriteria: A new command `analyze-interface` is registered in `App.RunAsync` and exposed through an `IRtCommand` implementation under `src/RoslynTools/Commands`.
The command accepts an interface symbol spec plus `--solution`, optional scope-filtering options, and a `--json` flag for structured output.

A new core implementation under `src/RoslynTools/Core` resolves the target interface symbol, finds its consumer types across the solution, and computes the exact interface members referenced by each consumer.
Output groups results by consuming type rather than by raw reference location.
For each consumer, the command lists the exact interface methods, properties, or events that are actually used by that consumer.
A consumer that references the interface type but does not invoke any members directly is still reported explicitly as a zero-member or type-only usage case rather than being silently dropped.
Member-usage analysis handles constructor-injected fields, local variables, parameters, and properties whose static type is the target interface.
The analysis excludes declaration-only references, `nameof()` references, and unrelated symbols with the same member name that do not bind to the target interface members.
An unresolved or non-interface symbol produces a clear validation error and exits non-zero.
Plain-text output is concise and grouped by consumer, and `--json` emits a stable structure containing the interface, consumer, usedMembers, and supporting metadata.

A test fixture covers: two consumers using different subsets of interface members, a consumer with no direct member calls, a consumer with type-only interface references, cross-file consumers, `nameof()` exclusion, non-interface validation, and JSON output shape.

acceptanceCriteria: `analyze-interface` gains an opt-in mode or flag that augments exact member-usage output with suggested minimal replacement interface shapes per consumer.

Consumers with identical used-member sets share the same suggested member-set signature or group identifier in the output.
The suggestion layer is derived solely from exact member-usage analysis results and does not invent members that were not observed in the underlying consumer analysis.
Suggestion output is clearly labeled as advisory and does not imply that a named interface type already exists in the solution.
If a consumer uses every member on the target interface, the output explicitly reports that no narrowing benefit exists for that consumer.
Plain-text output remains readable when suggestions are enabled, and JSON output includes a stable field for the suggested member set or replacement-interface signature.

userStories.title: narrow-dependency refactor workflow for interface segregation
userStories.description: As a developer, I want an assisted narrow-dependency refactor that extracts a smaller interface and updates consumers to the narrower type so that interface-segregation work becomes a safe tool-driven edit instead of a manual cross-file rewrite.
acceptanceCriteria: A new mutation command or command family is added that can extract a selected subset of members from an existing interface into a new interface type.
The command accepts the source interface, the selected member list, the new interface name, `--solution`, and `--dry-run` options at minimum.
The new interface file is created in the appropriate namespace, or an existing interface is reused when the requested target already exists and matches the selected shape.
The source interface is updated so that it extends or otherwise remains compatible with the newly extracted narrower interface when that relationship is requested by the command design.

Consumer classes that only require the selected subset are rewritten so constructor parameters, backing fields, and obvious local type annotations use the narrower interface instead of the original wider one.
Consumers that still require members outside the selected subset are left unchanged and are reported explicitly in the command output.
DI registration updates are out of scope for v1 of this story; command output may report likely manual DI follow-up when consumer types were narrowed.
If the selected member list contains a member that is not on the source interface, the command fails with a clear validation error and makes no changes.
If narrowing a specific consumer would be unsafe because its actual usage exceeds the selected member set, that consumer is skipped with an explicit reason rather than being partially rewritten.
Running with `--dry-run` prints a unified diff covering the new interface file, interface declarations, and any narrowed consumers, and writes no files to disk.
Running without `--dry-run` applies all validated changes via `SolutionWriter.ApplyChangesAsync` and creates any new files needed.

Tests cover: extracting a new interface from an existing wider interface, narrowing a consumer whose usage matches the subset, leaving a mixed-usage consumer unchanged, invalid-member validation, dry-run behavior, and explicit reporting that DI updates remain manual in v1.

userStories.title: extract-class safety validation and dependency-injection reuse
userStories.description: As a developer, I want `rt extract-class` to reject unsafe extractions and reuse a single dependency-injection implementation so that the command does not generate broken code on non-trivial classes.
acceptanceCriteria: `ExtractClassCommand` resolves the target source type semantically and fails with a clear validation error when `--type` is ambiguous across the loaded solution.

Extracting from a field declaration that declares multiple variables (for example `private int a, b;`) either splits the declaration safely or rejects the extraction with a clear validation error; it must never remove unrelated variables.
Before moving members, the command performs semantic validation of the selected members and detects references to source-class instance state that will not exist on the extracted type.

If any selected member references a non-extracted instance field, property, method, or `this`-bound member that would make the extracted type invalid, the command exits non-zero with an actionable error and makes no partial changes.
A safe extraction where all required state is self-contained or fully extracted continues to produce the new class file and remove the selected members from the source type.

The logic that injects the extracted type back into the source class reuses the shared core `DependencyInjector` implementation rather than keeping a second divergent nested implementation in `AddDependencyCommand`.

The shared `DependencyInjector` exposes a reliable applied/no-op signal so callers can distinguish `class not found`, `already injected`, and `rewrite applied` cases without duplicating syntax checks.

`DependencyInjector` matches existing constructor dependencies structurally rather than by `string.Contains(...)`, so qualified type names, aliases, and similarly named types do not produce false positives.

Expression-bodied constructors are either rewritten correctly to assign the injected field or explicitly rejected with a clear validation error; the command must not add a parameter without adding the assignment.
Running `extract-class --dry-run` still prints a unified diff to stdout and writes no files when validation passes, and writes no files when validation fails.

A new or updated test fixture covers: ambiguous source-type resolution, rejection of extraction that captures a non-extracted instance field, multi-variable field extraction safety, successful safe extraction, reuse of the shared `DependencyInjector`, structural duplicate-dependency detection, and expression-bodied-constructor handling.

userStories.title: make-instance reachability ambiguity and scope-awareness hardening

acceptanceCriteria: `InstanceReachabilityAnalyzer.FindReachableInstance` returns an explicit no-match/ambiguous result when more than one reachable field or property of the target type exists on the enclosing type; it must not silently pick the first member returned by Roslyn.
When multiple parameters of the target type are in scope on the enclosing callable, the analyzer reports ambiguity instead of selecting the first parameter.
When multiple local variables of the target type are reachable before the call site in the same block, the analyzer reports ambiguity instead of selecting the first declaration.
The analyzer continues to reject static contexts: it must never return `this` or an instance field/property from a static method or static constructor.

Local reachability analysis handles at least these additional declaration shapes: `using var`, `foreach (var x in ...)`, and deconstruction locals when the declared symbol type matches the target type.
If a declaration shape cannot be analyzed safely, the analyzer falls back to 'no reachable instance' rather than guessing.
`MakeInstanceCore` surfaces ambiguous reachability distinctly in warning output so skipped call sites report `ambiguous reachable instance` instead of the generic `no reachable instance` reason.
Multiple skipped call sites in the same document are still rewritten in a single pass without later replacements using stale spans from earlier edits.
